name: Gareth Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Hollins Farm for the Marlowe family trust, about 380 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, plus 110 suckler cows. I'm up at half five, check the cows and the calving pens, then sit down with my phone and a coffee and plan the day for Piotr (our tractor driver) and Kezia, our apprentice. Most of the day I'm out there myself: drilling, spraying, moving cattle, fixing whatever broke overnight. I live in the farm cottage that comes with the job, so the farm is never really off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a field right, a clean even crop you can see from the road, and I like teaching Kezia, who's sharp. What wears me out is the money side. Pay for farm managers round here is low, I've got less than a month's wages put by, and the trust's accountant questions every invoice. I use AI on my phone every day now, for the monthly report to the trustees, spray records, and checking cattle rations, and honestly it's given me back an evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and not much more. At the farmers' meeting in the pub I'd tell them I still use it for the paperwork and that's that. Nobody would argue, half of them never touched it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays as tight as it is now. The job is safe enough, but I'm on a one-year contract with the trust, the cottage goes with the job, and Edward Marlowe (the trust's chairman) keeps asking whether the arable would be cheaper with a contractor. AI fizzling out doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the AI for the reports since it already saves me time, and put a bit more effort into proving Hollins is well run. This winter I'd try to put aside fifty pounds a week into a separate account, because a broken car would wipe us out today. I'd also ask the trust again about a small rise when the contract comes up in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady, with a knot underneath. Nothing about AI worries me in that picture. What worries me is being 58 in a house I don't own, with no real savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the cottage. What would happen if the trust ever let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama (my wife) and I would have three months to find somewhere to live, which is what the contract says. I'm 58, I live in a house that comes with my job, and I've got less than a month's wages in the bank. AI fizzling out doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan would go first, then probably the phone contract. Food and the electricity stay paid, always. Ama's school kitchen job covers the shopping, and my wage covers everything else, just.

say: I'd call AI a **handy tool** for paperwork and not much else.
I'd tell neighbours at the pub that **nothing has changed** on the land.
think: My **job feels safe enough**, but I'm on a one-year contract.
The **tied cottage** means losing the job would also mean losing our home.
AI fizzling out does nothing for my **thin savings** or low pay.
do: Keep using **AI for reports**, since it already saves an evening a week.
Put aside **fifty pounds a week** into a separate account this winter.
Ask the trust for a **small pay rise** when the contract renews in March.
feel: A **knot of worry** about age, housing and having almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for farms that are willing to learn, and I'd mean it. I'd tell the lads at the machinery dealer that the paperwork side of farming is about to get a lot lighter. Online I'd probably post something about how I already do the trust's reports in a quarter of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it helps me more than it hurts me, at least for a few years. The thinking part of my job is maybe a quarter of it: the grain selling, the spray plans, the reports. Robots aren't close to calving a cow in a storm, so the hands-on half of my job buys me a few years at Hollins Farm. The risk is that the trust decides a cheaper manager with good software would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever farm-planning software the co-op offers and get properly good at it within the first six months. I'd write down for the trustees exactly what I save them, in hours and in pounds, so they see me as the person who makes the tools pay. I'd also teach Kezia to use it, because if she can run it too, the farm doesn't need an outside consultant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, even a bit excited. Underneath there's the same worry about being replaceable, but in this picture I feel like I'm ahead of the queue, not at the back of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Piotr or Kezia, not yet, they're hands-on. I'd worry about Margaret, who does the paperwork at the grain co-op, and the young agronomist (a crop adviser) who comes round every month. If software writes the spray plans, the trust stops paying for his visits, and he's got two little kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. What would make you wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Edward Marlowe looked at it and thought a twenty-five-year-old with an app could do my job for less, I'd be wrong. Experience matters on a farm, but trustees in an office don't always see it. I'd be hoping my numbers spoke for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we've all got to be the ones running the machines, not the ones run over by them. I'd say it at the co-op meeting and to the trustees. I'd also say government had better sort out pensions quickly, because nobody planned for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's frightening because of the dates. By 2028 the AI can do all my planning and selling, so my manager role is half gone straight away, and by 2031 the robots can drill and calve too, when I'm 63, four years short of my pension. And when the job goes, the cottage goes, so it's not just money, it's where Ama and I live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go to the trustees and offer to run the changeover myself: buying the robots, setting them up, being the one human on site. I'd try to get a written promise that the cottage stays mine until 67, even at lower pay. I'd cut the car loan by selling the newer car and keeping the old van. And I'd ask Tobi (our son, who works in IT) to help me learn whatever systems the robot firms use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor has a crack in it. I'm usually the one who sees change coming and gets ahead of it, but two years doesn't give you room to get ahead of anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which matters more to you, the job or the cottage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cottage, no question. I can find work fixing robots or driving a delivery van if I have to. When the farm manager job goes, the cottage goes with it. So for Ama (my wife) and me, it isn't only about money, it's about where we sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight: we've got two years before the office side goes and five before the field side does, and I've got a plan, but no guarantee. Then I'd probably ring Adaeze (our daughter) and ask if her spare room is still free, just in case. Ama would say I'm too calm, and she'd be right.

I'd push government to **sort out pensions** fast, since nobody planned for this.
think: By 2028 AI takes my **planning and selling**, so half my role goes.

fieldNote: He splits the threat clearly: **thinking work in 2028**, hands-on work in 2031.
His instinct is to **sell himself** as the robot supervisor, not to resist.
The **tied cottage** turns a job worry into a housing worry.
Composed voice, but he admits two years is **too short** for his usual strategy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people start now. At the co-op I'd tell the younger farmers to learn the systems and the older ones to sort out their pensions. Online I'd probably say less, because people get angry about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the same end, but the dates land better for me. AGI arrives in 2031 when I'm 63, and the robots for field work around 2034, when I'm 66 and nearly at my state pension. So the thinking side of my job, the planning and reports, goes when I'm 63, but my hands keep me on the farm till close to retirement. Five years also lets me fix the cottage problem before it bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start saving properly, a hundred pounds a week once the car loan is cleared next summer. I'd talk to the trust about a written deal: I stay as manager through the changeover, and they let us rent the cottage at a fair price after I retire. I'd also do a short course on farm robotics at the agricultural college, evenings, so I'm the one they call when the machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much better than the two-year one. Uneasy, because the end is the same, but I can see a path from here to 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the hands-on part of your job give you that the office part doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mostly. The office side of my job goes when I'm 63 and the field side when I'm 66. Those three years in between are my bridge to the pension. And frankly, the hands-on part is the bit I'm best at, I can tell a sick calf from forty metres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the agricultural college course. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one I've looked at is about four hundred pounds for twelve evenings. That's a lot for us, but I'd ask the trust to pay half, since they'd get the benefit. If they said no, I'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and nobody has an excuse not to prepare. At the trust meetings I'd push for a ten-year plan for Hollins. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, ten years mostly means I retire before it really hits. I'd be 68 when AGI arrives and 71 when the robots come, so the farm will change after I've gone. Ten years is the gentlest version for me, but it's the one where I lie awake about Kezia (our apprentice) and my son instead of myself. Tobi's IT job is exactly the kind of thinking work that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and keep building the savings slowly, a hundred pounds a week. I'd sit down with Kezia this winter and help her plan: get her robotics and machinery certificates now, so she's the one running the machines in 2039. And I'd tell the trustees to start putting money aside for robots in the 2030s rather than borrowing for them later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about myself, mostly, but uneasy for the young ones. It's odd, ten years is the gentlest version but it's the one where I worry most about other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about the cottage in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but differently. The cottage goes when I retire whatever happens with AI, and with almost nothing saved, Ama and I would need a cheap rental. That's an old worry, not a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tobi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tobi he's got ten years, and that the people who'll still have work are the ones who can fix things with their hands as well as their heads. Maybe he should look at the robot servicing side. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd listen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because the robots come when I'm 63 and the cottage goes with the job. What would help is a law that farm workers in tied housing get a fair chance to stay on as tenants when the job goes. A bit of help paying for robotics training for people my age would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. On a farm like Hollins, the trust will own the robots and keep the savings, and the workers will get nothing from it. I don't blame Edward Marlowe for that, it's just how it works, but somebody should be thinking about it.
